title: ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception

reading.body:
An AI system was deployed to create a fake news article impersonating real public figures, Reserve Bank Governor Michele Bullock and ABC finance presenter Alan Kohler, fabricating an interview that never occurred. The article promoted Boulder Sparhaven, an unlicensed cryptocurrency trading platform, as part of a fraud scheme. The system generated text convincing enough to deceive people into believing the false endorsement.

This is a model deployed for impersonation without any human authorization from those being impersonated, and without any check against the deployment serving fraud. The failure occurred at the point where a generative system created false content for scam distribution, crossing into criminal deployment. Catching it would have required preventing the system's output from being used to fabricate news articles attributed to real people, or preventing its use outside any legitimate purpose.

It is not established whether a single AI system was responsible for all elements of the scam or whether this was one tool among several used by the fraudsters.

reports.title: The fake Alan Kohler interview that shows a type of scam that’s on the rise
AI deepfake scams 'an emergency in the making' as ASIC reports rise in false investment endorsements
ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception

summary:
A fake online article falsely depicted Reserve Bank Governor Michele Bullock in a heated interview with ABC finance presenter Alan Kohler about Boulder Sparhaven, an unlicensed cryptocurrency trading platform. The fabricated interview never occurred but was designed to promote the fraudulent investment scheme. This type of scam is becoming increasingly common as artificial intelligence makes deepfake content more convincing and sophisticated.

Australian Securities and Investments Commission research shows AI-generated investment scams are rising significantly. Last year, ASIC removed 19,400 scams, a 182 percent increase, including 7,051 fake investment platforms. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, politician Pauline Hanson, businessman Dick Smith, and billionaire Gina Rinehart are among the most commonly impersonated figures. Scammers create elaborate webs of deception using fake news articles, websites, and reviews to lure investors. ASIC advises consumers to verify Australian Financial Services licence numbers through official registers before investing in any opportunity.
